question.:question/problem: Given that $f(r,\theta)=3 r^{3}$, find $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$, where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{∂f}{∂r}\sin \theta+\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta}\cos \theta.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r}=9 r^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂\theta}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(9 r^{2})\sin \theta+\frac{1}{r}(0)\cos \theta \\ & =9 r^{2} \sin {\theta}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: r>0; real theta on any locally continuous polar angle branch; x=r*cos(theta), y=r*sin(theta).

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(3 \cos {4 \theta})\sin \theta+\frac{1}{r}(- 12 r \sin {4 \theta})\cos \theta \\ & =3 \sin {\theta} \cos {4 \theta}- 12 \sin {4 \theta} \cos {\theta}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=- 3 r (\sin {\theta} + 3),$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂y}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\sin \theta+\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta}\cos \theta.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=- 3 \sin {\theta} - 9,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta}=- 3 r \cos {\theta}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂y} & =(- 3 \sin {\theta} - 9)\sin \theta+\frac{1}{r}(- 3 r \cos {\theta})\cos \theta \\ & =-3\sin^{2} \theta-9\sin \theta-3\cos^{2} \theta \\ & =- 9 \sin {\theta} - 3.\end{aligned}
$$
